entities.name: Alexander de Brus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Alexander de Brus, Dean of Glasgow, was a pivotal, albeit short-lived, figure in the early stages of the First War of Scottish Independence (1296–1328), serving as a crucial ecclesiastical and familial supporter of his elder brother, Robert I of Scotland. Born into the powerful Bruce family, likely in the latter half of the 13th century, Alexander's commitment to his brother's claim to the Scottish throne in 1306 placed him squarely in opposition to King Edward I of England, a stance that ultimately led to his brutal execution in 1307. His significance lies in his immediate and unwavering loyalty to Robert Bruce at a time when the nascent rebellion desperately needed legitimization and internal cohesion against overwhelming English might.

Following Robert Bruce's audacious murder of John Comyn in February 1306 and his subsequent coronation at Scone, Alexander swiftly abandoned his clerical duties to join his brother's precarious campaign. He was entrusted with vital diplomatic missions to Ireland, seeking military support, and likely served as a morale booster within the small, embattled Bruce retinue. However, his active participation was tragically cut short in February 1307 when, returning from Ireland with supplies and reinforcements, his ship was forced ashore at Loch Ryan in Galloway. There, he was captured by the forces of Dungal Macdowall, a staunch Comyn loyalist and supporter of the English cause, alongside his younger brother Thomas de Brus and other key Bruce adherents.
